Learning Objectives
Apply the principles of medical ethics.
Determine general issues of professionalism and issues specific to orthopaedic surgeons.
Principles of Medical Ethics
Overview
Four principles of medical ethics: respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice
Prima facie duty: duty that always is to be acted on unless it conflicts on a particular occasion
with an equal or stronger duty




Overview
The Nuremberg Code of 1948 was the first international code of ethics to be put forth.
This code came about after the Nazi trials and medical tribunals of the physicians who
participated in the medical trials. This code focused on research involving human
subjects. In the United States, the Belmont Report was written in 1979. It focused on
“ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research” and
put forth three basic ethical principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.1 In
1979, Beauchamp and Childress published the first edition of their book Principles of
Biomedical Ethics. This book built on the work of the Belmont Report with the addition of
the principle of nonmaleficence and a change from “respect for persons” to “respect for
autonomy.” These principles are nonhierarchical, and physicians have a prima facie duty
to uphold them2 (Resource 1).
Respect for Autonomy

Respect for Autonomy
The principle of respect for autonomy requires that physicians respect the autonomous
decisions of rational individuals. This principle is the foundation for informed consent.
For a patient to have capacity for this type of decision making, he or she must be able to
act intentionally, with understanding, and without controlling influences.
Beneficence

Beneficence
The principle of beneficence means that physicians have a duty to work to the patient’s
benefit. This principle is the most clear and obvious of the principles, and it lies at the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
2/21

heart of the healthcare relationship—that the physician will work to promote the
patient’s good.
Nonmaleficence

Nonmaleficence
The principle of nonmaleficence requires physicians to avoid intentionally creating harm
or injury to their patients. Acts of omission and commission are considered in this
principle. For example, a physician upholds this principle by providing appropriate
perioperative antibiotic agents.
Occasionally, nonmaleficence has been considered as a core principle, made famous by
the aphorism “primum non nocere,” or “first, do no harm.” This phrase did not appear in
the Hippocratic Oath and was instead likely written in the 17th century by Thomas
Sydenham, an English physician. This core value is intended to give a physician pause
before automatically recommending surgical management (which may result in
complications), prescribing a medicine (which may result in adverse effects), or ordering
a test (which may show false-positive results, provoking anxiety or resulting in
inappropriate management).
Justice

Justice
Dissimilar from the first three principles, which function at the level of the individual
patient-physician relationship, the principle of justice functions at a societal level. The
principle of justice holds that patients in similar positions should be treated in a similar
manner. An example of this principle is observed in the Medicare program, which is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
3/21

available to all individuals older than 65 years and for all individuals with kidney failure
who require dialysis.
Professionalism
Overview
Professionalism builds on these basic principles to create codes of professional conduct.
Multiple codes of professional ethics exist, including those from the American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons3 and the American Medical Association4 (Resources 2 and 3).
Codes of Ethics

Code of Ethics
The first code of medical ethics was the Hippocratic Oath. Most physicians adhere to an
updated version written by Louis Lasagna in 1964. A fundamental tenet of
professionalism is that the patient’s interests should always be foremost. Maintaining
this principle may be a challenge in a fee-for-service medical environment, in which
volume- and price-related incentives may affect decision making.
Modern professional codes include an emphasis on privacy (which, in the United States,
is codified in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996) and patient
empowerment (informed consent). Modern professionalism also assumes good medical
record keeping and accurate billing.
Informed Consent
Informed consent is predicated on the respect for persons and their right to make
autonomous decisions.
Informed consent depends on providing adequate information so that the patient can make a
decision regarding which therapeutic option to follow or whether to enroll in a research study.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
4/21


Informed Consent
Informed consent is based on the principle of respect for autonomy. Autonomous
decision making involves three components for processes requiring consent: (1) the
patient must have capacity, (2) the patient must have the knowledge and understanding
required to make the decision (ie, be informed), and (3) the consent must be voluntary.5
From a practical perspective, physicians must present alternate treatment options,
describe the risks and advantages of each treatment option, and use language that is
clear and free of jargon6 (Resource 4).
Most of the clinical consent process is oral. The written document should highlight the
most important aspects made during the oral discussion. The physician obtaining
consent should make a good faith effort to evaluate whether the patient understands
the information that has been provided. Patients have the right to decide their own
course of treatment, even if their decisions are bad from the point of view of a physician.
In addition, patients should be aware that their decision to proceed with treatment is
voluntary.
In clinical care, deciding whether written consent or oral consent is required usually is
based on risk. For most invasive procedures, written consent is expected. For minor
procedures (eg, phlebotomy), consent usually is tacit (understood) or oral. Written
informed consent underscores the point to the practitioner and the patient that a
serious decision is being made.
True informed consent requires three key elements: the provision of adequate
information, comprehension of the information by the person being asked to consent,
and voluntariness.
Complications and the Peer Review Process
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
5/21

Complications are an inevitable but hopefully rare consequence of surgical management.
The possibility of complications should be addressed during the informed consent process.
A balance should be struck between describing meaningful risks and providing an all-inclusive
list of potential problems.
Recent research suggests that directly admitting mistakes that have caused complications
prevents malpractice suits more effectively than evasion or avoiding discussion with the
patient or the patient’s family.
Peer Review
If a mistake is made, peer review is an important teaching and evaluative tool.
Peer review and other forms of quality improvement are legally protected in most states;
however, slanderous and inaccurate statements made during the review process are not
protected. Transparently false accusations may result in peer-based condemnation of the
accuser.
To be successful, peer review should focus on teaching rather than retribution.
The best peer review looks forward, providing solutions that will prevent problems in the
future.
In addition, good peer review considers system issues and individual physician performance.
Industry Relationships
Types of Relationships
Medical research relationships with industry are not intrinsically bad.7
Physician-industry relationships fall into several categories: employment, scientific
collaborations, clinical, and marketing (Resource 5).

Types of Relationships
Industry may sponsor research by a physician or group of physicians. In academic
medical centers, research contracts generally are agreements between the institution
and the company, whereas for physicians in private practice, the contract usually is
between the practice and the sponsor or contract research organization.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
6/21

Contracts with academic medical centers are more complicated because universities, as
nonprofit entities, must work in the public benefit. In research, that usually means
assurance that the work will be published. In addition, many academic medical centers
include language in their contracts that allows them to retain the rights to new
intellectual property. Because private practices rarely pay attention to either of these
issues, those practices have contractual advantages from the point of view of many
sponsors.
Risks of Relationships
Industry-sponsored research is associated with a risk of bias.

Risks of Relationships
To minimize the potential for bias, physician-researchers working with industry and
charged with writing any study-related manuscripts should request access to the raw
research data; however, this is not the industry research norm.
Close relationships with industry may produce bias, particularly if personal
compensation depends on a particular outcome. For example, if a physician invents and
then licenses a product, resulting in a royalty stream, positive results from a study of
that product may increase the inventor’s personal income. This type of relationship may
reduce the credibility of the research if the inventor takes a key role. Biased research
results also may be harmful to future patients.
Management of Conflicts of Interest
The Physician Payments Sunshine Act requires reporting of payments to physicians and
academic medical centers.
Research sponsored by the National Institutes of Health has special reporting requirements.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
7/21


Management of Conflicts of Interest
As of 2013, the Physician Payments Sunshine Act (part of the Affordable Care Act of
2010) requires pharmaceutical companies, device manufacturers, and medical service
providers to report all payments of $10 or more made to physicians and academic
medical centers. These reports are summarized in a publicly accessible, searchable
website so all physician-industry financial arrangements become public knowledge.
Beyond these disclosures, physicians are ethically obligated to disclose financial or
ownership interests to patients. This includes relationships with durable medical goods,
surgery centers, or imaging centers if such relationships are not immediately apparent
to the patient. Physicians must disclose royalty relationships to patients if a physician
plans to use a royalty-generating device in a patient.
For National Institutes of Health grants, the US Public Health Service requires reporting
of all major financial interests that may directly and substantially affect the design,
conduct, or reporting of research. This responsibility falls on the institution that receives
the grant, usually an academic institution or nonprofit organization. To help the
institution identify which financial interests to report, investigators are required to fully
disclose their financial relationships. After those relationships are disclosed to the
institution, the conflict-of-interest program is expected to manage any conflicts.
Typical management strategies include a requirement for disclosure of external financial
relationships. Institutional review boards (IRBs) often require that informed consent
documents provide information about external financial interests. The National
Institutes of Health expects the institution to describe how its management approach
will mitigate the effects of conflict-of-interest–related bias in the research. The institution
is required to file a formal report with the US Public Health Service.
Disclosures of Industry Relationships
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
8/21

A potential conflict of interest exists if the professional judgment about the patient’s well-being
has a reasonable chance of being influenced by other interests of the physician.8

Disclosures of Industry Relationships
Cooperative relationships between physicians and industry are important for scientific
advancement; however, potential for conflict of interests exists if a physician has
financial interests that may weigh on their professional judgments about patient care.
Physicians must disclose this conflict to patients, the public, and colleagues. If a conflict
exists that cannot be resolved, the orthopaedic surgeon must consult with colleagues or,
ideally, an institutional ethics committee on how to proceed. The orthopaedic surgeon is
a fiduciary to his or her patients; therefore, he or she must always act in the patient’s
best interests. Any potential conflict of interest must be resolved in the best interest of
the patient.
The Ethics of Gainsharing
Gainsharing, sometimes called pay for performance, is a contracted relationship in which
physicians are incentivized to decrease costs without compromising the quality of care.
Ethical concerns about gainsharing agreements focus on the potential for undue influence of
the financial incentives (ie, that physicians will reduce or limit services because of financial
services).
Gainsharing arrangements may be ethical given that the patient’s best interests remain
paramount and all regulatory and legal constructs are followed.11
Gainsharing arrangements for the bundling of orthopaedic care incentivize decreased
complications, which may lead to cherry-picking for healthy patients and less access for racial
minorities and individuals of lower socioeconomic status.

The Ethics of Gainsharing
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
9/21

Gainsharing agreements have shown promise as a mechanism to reduce healthcare
costs without compromising the quality of care. These programs can be designed in
multiple ways, for example, implant cost reduction.9 Programs have showed promise in
reducing hospital length of stay.10
Incentive structures are associated with the potential for undue inducement (ie, that
profit motives will motivate physicians to provide inappropriate care). Frequently, this
ethical issue is considered in the context of offering excessive or inappropriate care for
increased compensation (eg, a surgeon who inappropriately provides cash-only stem cell
injections for end-stage arthritis). In contrast to this situation of overusing nonbeneficial
treatment for profit, the ethical concerns about gainsharing focus on underuse of
beneficial treatments so physicians will financially benefit from cost savings.
The Office of the Inspector General issued guidance in 1999, suggesting that gainsharing
arrangements were illegal. This position was reversed in 2005. The Centers for Medicare
& Medicaid Services was given Congressional approval to develop gainsharing programs
with safeguards. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services then introduced
gainsharing agreements into the 2010 Bundled Payments for Care Improvement
Initiative, which included bundled payments for total joint arthroplasty. These programs
were designed to function within strong safeguards and continuing legal review. Beyond
the legal framework, orthopaedic surgeons must continue to maintain their ethically
required duties to their patients’ best interests.
Gainsharing agreements are designed to incentivize increased quality of care. The
primary metric for measuring quality is decreased surgical complications and
readmissions. Patients who are healthier preoperatively are less likely to have
complications and readmissions; however, good health is not equitably distributed in
society. Risk factors for increased complications after hip and knee replacement include
higher body mass index, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and smoking, with racial
minorities and individuals of lower socioeconomic status more likely to have these risk
factors.12 Evidence exists that African American patients have increased episode-of-care
costs after total hip replacement and total knee replacement compared with Caucasian
patients.13 Policy makers and orthopaedic surgeons must consider the potential for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
10/21

bundled payments and gainsharing agreements to worsen existing healthcare disparities
in designing these programs.
Research Ethics
Overview
Medical research often involves some level of risk—known and unknown—to the participants.
Therefore, the nature of research requires specific codes of ethics and unique obligations of
researchers to their research participants.
Sponsored Research
Each institution has its own research requirements; however, specific requirements exist for
certain types of sponsored research.

Sponsored Research
Federally sponsored research is regulated by the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
Regulation 45 CFR §46, known as the Common Rule, also is applied to most other human
investigation in the United States. The FDA has its own set of rules, set down in
regulation 21 CFR §50 and §56, that are similar to the Common Rule but add
requirements related to FDA jurisdiction. The Common Rule is based largely on the
Belmont Report, a 1979 document written by the National Commission for the
Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. This commission
was created in response to several research scandals, including the Tuskegee syphilis
study, in which investigators appeared to prioritize scientific objectives over the health
and well-being of the individuals who took part in the research. In some instances, the
study participants were neither aware nor even informed that they were involved in
research.
Institutional Review Boards
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
11/21

IRBs evaluate research protocols for scientific validity, ethical design, and proposed conduct14
(Resource 6).

Institutional Review Boards
The Belmont Report codified three basic principles for the ethical conduct of clinical
research: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Respect for persons holds that
individuals have autonomous rights to participate (or not) in research, and their
decisions should be made based on an informed consent process. Beneficence requires
that the research should benefit the participants in the research or individuals similar to
them. Finally, justice means that the selection of research participants should be fair.
Before human participants are enrolled in a research study in the United States, the
research proposal should be submitted to an IRB for review. Internationally, most
institutions and countries have ethics review boards that serve the same function as
IRBs.
Specific Issues in Medical Ethics
Culturally Competent Care
Because many medical decisions involve issues surrounding values, physicians should be
aware that diverse cultures may have different priorities.
Patients must understand their diagnosis and treatment options. A medical translator is
required if the patient and physician speak different languages.

Culturally Competent Care
Before a patient makes an important medical decision, the clinical team should help the
patient achieve a full understanding of the critical issues. Knowledge of the patient’s
diagnosis and treatment options is required to support autonomous decision making.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
12/21

In some situations, if a physician does not agree with a decision made by the patient, the
physician may decide not to continue to participate in providing care for that patient. A
physician who so chooses still has a moral and legal obligation to ensure that another
care provider is arranged for or to give the patient adequate time to find alternative
care.
A patient who does not speak the same language as the physician will require a
translator who is sufficiently skilled so that medical information can be conveyed
accurately. Privacy concerns should be considered in selecting a translator, particularly if
the potential translator is a friend or family member of the patient because many
patients do not want their clinical status made public.
The physician should be aware that some patients may perceive a power imbalance
between the patient and the physician. They may believe that they should accede to the
physician’s instructions solely because of the physician’s authority rather than because
they agree with the physician’s treatment plan. Although this behavior may be
convenient for the physician, in medical care, the goal should be voluntary consent
rather than simple compliance.
Elder Abuse and Child Abuse
A physician who encounters evidence of potential elder abuse or child abuse (eg, multiple
poorly explained fractures in a single child) is required by law in almost all states to report
their concerns to the local social service agency.

Elder Abuse and Child Abuse
Physicians are mandatory reporters for elder and child abuse. Elder abuse is an
intentional act or failure to act that causes or creates a risk of harm to an older adult
(age =60 years).15 The federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act defines child
abuse and neglect as “any recent act or failure to act on the part of a parent or caregiver
that results in death, serious physical or emotional harm, sexual abuse or exploitation,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
13/21

or an act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm”16
(Resources 7 and 8).
Deciding to report elder abuse or child abuse may be difficult because the act of
reporting may rupture the therapeutic relationship between the patient, the family, and
the medical provider. The highest priority is established by law; the person at risk should
be protected. Reporting suspected elder abuse or child abuse is protected by law. Only
in situations of malicious reporting is the person filing the report legally liable.
Conversely, failure to report is a potentially negligent act under the law.
End-of-Life Issues
Advance care directives or living wills can guide the care team in patients with incapacitating
illness17 (Resource 9).
A medical power of attorney can serve as a decision maker for a patient who is incapacitated.

End-of-Life Issues
Most states allow the use of advance care directives (also called a living will). These
documents allow an individual to specify his or her expectations in the case of
incapacitating medical illness, particularly situations in which the person is not able to
express his or her wishes (eg, regarding feeding tubes, intubation, chest compressions).
Advance care directives are especially useful for patients with diseases such as cancer or
progressive dementia. They also can facilitate conversation within a family regarding an
individual’s preferences about end-of-life decisions. An advance care directive is not
binding. Unanticipated circumstances may occur (eg, a need for short-term intubation
for a surgical procedure), and family members may not agree with the patient. The
physician should encourage the family to observe the spirit of the advance directive;
however, a living family member (who can sue) may make it difficult to follow the paper
advance care directive. Most advance care directives lack adequate granularity to answer
all questions that may arise. For example, did the now-comatose patient intend to
exclude feeding tubes or only intubation? What is the realistic probability of recovery?
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
14/21

For patients who have dementia or who anticipate periods in which they may not be able
to make decisions (eg, postoperatively), assigning a medical power of attorney is
important. The designee may be a family member, a friend, or an advocate. The person
with medical power of attorney should pay close attention to the wishes of the patient as
much as possible. A medical power of attorney is empowered to make healthcare
decisions for an incapacitated patient.
Care of the Uninsured
Physicians are not required by law to provide care for the uninsured.
Hospitals are required to provide emergency care for individuals who need it, regardless of the
patient’s ability to pay.

Care of the Uninsured
Physicians are not legally required to provide care for the uninsured. As the population
of medically indigent increases, physicians are increasingly challenged by how to best
care for individuals without health insurance. Failure to pay bills is not adequate reason
to immediately terminate a patient in need of continued care; however, it may prompt a
notification advising the patient to seek other care providers. The physician or practice
should give the patient adequate time to arrange alternative care. Physicians are
permitted to require cash payments in their practice settings.
Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act, hospitals must, in
general, provide emergency care for individuals who need it, regardless of the patient’s
ability to pay. Hospitals can require physicians to provide emergency care as part of their
work contract with the hospital.
Patients who do not have the means to pay for care may require more careful discharge
planning. For example, an elderly patient who has a fracture that suggests osteoporosis
should be referred for the management of bone mineral density to prevent an avoidable
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
15/21

second fracture. A patient who lacks financial resources may need to be referred to a
publicly funded clinic.
Sports Medicine Issues
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 does not cover physicians
employed by a team in their communication with the team18 (Resource 10).
Return-to-play decisions should be made conservatively, and a player who loses consciousness
should not be returned to play without a full evaluation.19 (Resource 11).

Sports Medicine Issues
Physicians engaged in sports medicine, particularly the care of professional athletes,
often are caught in a conflict-of-interest situation in that their employer is the team and
their patients are the athletes who play for the team. The team physician is part of the
team. Good medical care requires the confidence of the patient/player, including
confidence in the privacy of information.
The rules surrounding privacy may not be clear in a team setting. The Health Insurance
Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 generally does not cover physicians employed
by a team in their communication with the team. Therefore, confidentiality decisions
mainly reflect professional ethics and personal discretion rather than legal principles.
Some decisions pit the player’s best interests against those of the team. A decision to
play despite the risk of long-term injury should be made by a fully informed player who
has received independent advice. Players should be allowed to seek second opinions
from independent physicians.
Return-to-play decisions should be made conservatively, particularly after a head injury.
Players may lack capacity because a head injury may prevent full understanding. If a
patient has lost consciousness, he or she should not be returned to play without a full
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:41 PM
AAOS | Medical Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001023
16/21

evaluation. Confusion after a head injury should prompt a careful evaluation. Players
often cannot judge their own medical condition after a head injury.
Preparticipation examination may reveal conditions that place an athlete at increased
risk for injury or sudden death. If such a health condition exists, a physician is
responsible for ensuring that adequate treatment is obtained to permit play or, in
certain circumstances, the athlete is disqualified from play.
